workflows.title: Read the Brief
workflows.summary: Restate the client's brief in technical terms, map what goes in and out, and log every question it leaves open.

steps.title: Restate the ask & its capabilities
steps.ask: Read the client brief I've pasted. Restate the ask in one sentence a developer would write — what must happen, with no technology named — then list the capabilities it implies as numbered verbs. If the brief names a technology, record it separately as a client preference.

lenses.note: Capabilities as verbs, with no technology chosen.

steps.title: Map inputs, outputs & volumes
steps.ask: From the same brief, list every input and output with its format (email, PDF, API call, file, screen…), the users who touch the system, and the volumes and peaks. Put the source next to every number, or mark it 'assumed'. End with an in-scope / out-of-scope list.

lenses.note: Every input and output has a format and a source.
Volumes and peaks written down with where they came from.

steps.title: Log the open technical questions
steps.ask: List every technical question the brief leaves open, as rows for my question log: Q-## ID, the question, its area (data, integration, performance, security, infrastructure, code), why it matters, and who could answer it. Mark any that only a spike or prototype can answer.

lenses.note: What can't we answer without the code or the client?
Which data is sensitive, and where may it live?

steps.title: Brief understood?
steps.ask: Compare my technical brief summary with the original brief. Point out anything I missed, misread or quietly turned into a solution — so I can take it to the tech lead for a read-back.

lenses.note: Could another engineer build the same thing from this summary?

steps.title: Give every question an owner
steps.ask: For each open question in my log, suggest the best person or source to answer it and the quickest way to get the answer. Flag any question that blocks tomorrow's work.

lenses.note: Every question has someone who can answer it.

loops: Conflicts with a hard limit → client

contract.definition: Restate the client's brief in technical terms, map what goes in and out, and log every question it leaves open.
decisions: Does the tech lead agree the brief is understood?
branches: Conflict with a hard limit → client
failures: Summary copies the brief instead of restating it
recovery: Rewrite each capability as a verb with an input and an output
Assign every question before the review closes

criteria: Every input and output has a format
contract.handoff: Technical brief summary & question log → 1.1.2 Audit the Current System & Codebase

objectives: Restate the ask without choosing a technology
List every input and output with its format
Turn every unknown into an owned question
lessons.exercise: Write the technical brief summary for the order-intake case: the one-line ask, five capabilities, inputs and outputs with formats, and three questions with owners. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: The brief says “use AI to read the orders”. How do you write the ask?
options: Use AI to read PDF orders
Turn emailed PDF orders into ERP orders without re-typing
Build an AI order bot
quiz.why: The ask says what must happen; “AI” is a client preference to record, not the requirement.

quiz.q: A volume in the brief has no source. What do you do?
options: Use it as given
Mark it assumed and log a question to confirm it
Leave it out
quiz.why: Numbers need a source or an assumption tag — they drive the design.

lessons.prompt:
I'm working through "Read the Brief as an Engineer" (Discover → Understand the Brief & the System) on my own project. Act as my assistant: draft and check, I decide.

Goal: Turn the client's brief into a precise technical understanding of what must be built — before choosing any solution.
Done looks like: A technical brief summary and a question log of every unknown, accepted by the tech lead.

I'll attach or paste: Client brief.

Work through these steps with me, one at a time:
1. Restate the ask & its capabilities → Technical brief summary
   Read the client brief I've pasted. Restate the ask in one sentence a developer would write — what must happen, with no technology named — then list the capabilities it implies as numbered verbs. If the brief names a technology, record it separately as a client preference.
2. Map inputs, outputs & volumes → Technical brief summary
   From the same brief, list every input and output with its format (email, PDF, API call, file, screen…), the users who touch the system, and the volumes and peaks. Put the source next to every number, or mark it 'assumed'. End with an in-scope / out-of-scope list.
3. Log the open technical questions → Technical question log
   List every technical question the brief leaves open, as rows for my question log: Q-## ID, the question, its area (data, integration, performance, security, infrastructure, code), why it matters, and who could answer it. Mark any that only a spike or prototype can answer.
4. Brief understood? (a decision — give me the options and a recommendation; I make the call)
   Compare my technical brief summary with the original brief. Point out anything I missed, misread or quietly turned into a solution — so I can take it to the tech lead for a read-back.
5. Give every question an owner → Technical question log
   For each open question in my log, suggest the best person or source to answer it and the quickest way to get the answer. Flag any question that blocks tomorrow's work.

Produce: Technical brief summary; Technical question log. Use clear headings I can paste into my document.

Before you finish, check it against: Ask stated without technology; Every input and output has a format; Volumes cite a source or are marked assumed.

Ask me for anything you need instead of guessing. Keep it specific to my project.

lessons.title: Audit the Current System & Codebase
lessons.summary: Run and read what exists today: components, stack, how it's built, code health and debt.

definition.purpose: Find out what really exists — by running and reading it — before proposing anything new.
definition.outcome: A system audit with components, stack, code health and debt, and a C4 context diagram.
definition.jtbd: Help me know what I'm building on, so I don't design around a system that doesn't exist.
entry: Read access to the repositories or a test environment
exit: System audit reviewed by the tech lead

normal: Get access and run the system
Follow one real transaction through the code
flow.stateTransitions: No access → Running → Traced → Measured → Reviewed

cases.happyPath: You can run it, the code is readable and the audit is accepted.
alternates: Greenfield — nothing built yet → audit the systems the new one must sit beside
edgeCases: Vendor system with no source code → audit its interfaces, configuration and docs
exceptions: Access is delayed → audit from docs and mark every finding unverified
failures: The system can be neither run nor read

routing.forward: System audit & context diagram → 1.1.3 Map Data, Integrations & Dependencies
routing.alternate: Greenfield → audit the neighbouring systems only
routing.rework: Unverified claims → run or read again
routing.escalation: Security issue found (e.g. secrets in code) → security owner the same day
routing.stop: System is being replaced anyway → stop auditing internals, keep its interfaces — recorded in the learning log

criteria: Findings come from running and reading the system
Every component has an ID and a version
checks: Tech lead review of the audit
policies: Security findings reported to their owner the same day

concerns: Designing around a system that doesn't exist
decisions: Can new work safely build on this?

agents: AI coding agent for reading the code
execution.authority: Tech lead accepts the audit; security owns any security finding.

workflows.title: Audit the System
workflows.summary: Run the system, follow one real transaction through the code, draw its context and measure its health — then judge whether new work can build on it.

steps.title: Get access & run the system
steps.ask: I have read access to this repository. Read the README, build files and dependency manifest, then give me the exact steps to run it locally or in a test environment. List anything that blocks running it.

lenses.note: Where does it run, and how is it deployed?
Logs, monitoring and backups — what exists?

steps.title: Follow one real transaction through the code
steps.ask: Follow one real transaction through the code — from its entry point to where data is stored and back — and list every component, class and external call it passes through, with file paths. Don't summarise the folder tree; follow the request.

lenses.note: Follow a real request, not the folder tree.
Which components does one transaction touch?

steps.title: Draw the system context
steps.ask: Draw a C4 level-1 context diagram as a table (element · type · talks to · protocol / format) for the system and everything around it: people, the system in scope, and every external system. Then give it to me as Mermaid too.

lenses.note: One box for the system in scope; every arrow named.
Mark every trust boundary you cross.

steps.title: Measure code health & debt
steps.ask: Measure the code's health with numbers: test count and coverage if available, dependencies and how far behind each is, build and deploy steps, TODO/FIXME count, duplicated logic. Then list the three debt hotspots that would slow new work, and any security finding (e.g. secrets in config) separately.

lenses.note: Tests and coverage as numbers.
Dependency age and build steps counted.

steps.title: Safe to build on?
steps.ask: From my audit, prepare the 'safe to build on?' call for the tech lead: build on it, build beside it, or replace it — the evidence for each, and what must be true first.

lenses.note: Build beside it, on it, or replace it — and why?

contract.definition: Run the system, follow one real transaction through the code, draw its context and measure its health — then judge whether new work can build on it.
decisions: Can new work safely build on this system, and on what conditions?
recovery: Mark each finding verified or unverified and verify the critical ones
Replace adjectives with counts: tests, dependency age, build steps
contract.rework: Unverified findings → run or read again
contract.handoff: System audit & context diagram → 1.1.3 Map Data, Integrations & Dependencies
traceability: Each component SYS-## linked to REQ-###
learning: Where the docs and the running system disagreed — learning log

objectives: Get a system running before judging it
Follow one real transaction through the code
lessons.exercise: Draw the C4 context for the order-intake case and write three code-health measures you would collect on erp-extensions. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: Where should a codebase audit start?
options: Reading every file in order
Running the system and following one real request
The architecture diagram on the wiki
quiz.why: The running system is the truth; a real request shows you the parts that matter.

quiz.q: You find ERP credentials hard-coded in config. What now?
options: Note it for the final report
Report it to the security owner the same day
Fix it quietly
quiz.why: Security findings go to their owner straight away — and you change nothing while auditing.

normal: Trace the data through today's flow
Review each contract and make a test call
dependencies: Test credentials for one real call

workflows.title: Map Data & Integrations
workflows.summary: Trace the data through today's flow, list every system and API the solution depends on, and prove each one with its real contract and a test call.

steps.title: Trace the data through today's flow
steps.ask: Trace the data through today's flow, as rows for my data flow map: DF-## ID, from, to, what data, format, trigger or frequency, volume, sensitivity (public / internal / personal / confidential), and whether a person does it by hand.

lenses.note: Where is data created, copied or re-typed?
Which flows carry personal data, and where do they go?

steps.title: List every integration & API
steps.ask: List every system, API and service the solution will depend on, as rows for my integration inventory: INT-## ID, direction, interface type, auth method, owner. Include the ones we'd have to add, such as a parsing or OCR service.

lenses.note: Every system the solution depends on.
Who owns each one, and what do they promise?

steps.title: Review contracts & make a test call
steps.ask: For each integration, read its real contract (OpenAPI spec, vendor guide or the calling code) and fill in: limits (rate, payload size, timeout, opening hours), error responses, idempotency and versioning. Write 'unknown' instead of guessing, and give me a single test call I can run against a test environment for each.

lenses.note: Rate, size and timeout limits as numbers.
How each call authenticates, and who issues the keys.

steps.title: Dependencies clear to proceed?
steps.ask: From my inventory, prepare the call for the tech lead: is any dependency blocking, which are high risk and why, and what would unblock each one.

lenses.note: Is any dependency a blocker?

steps.title: Record owners & follow-ups
steps.ask: For every unknown or high-risk row, draft the follow-up: who to ask, the exact question, and how it should come back (in writing, with a date). Add each as a question to my question log.

lenses.note: Follow-ups asked in writing, with a date.

loops: Limits or owners missing → review again

lessons.title: Log Technical Constraints & Assumptions
lessons.summary: Separate the limits you know from the ones you're assuming, and hand on one technical picture.

definition.purpose: Separate what you know about the system from what you're assuming, and hand on one consolidated technical picture.
definition.outcome: A technical constraint & assumption log and the system context pack, accepted by the tech lead.
definition.jtbd: Help me know which limits are real and which are guesses I still have to test.
entry: Data flow map and integration inventory reviewed

normal: Pull every limit from the brief, audit and integrations

exceptions: Owner unreachable → keep it as a low-confidence assumption
failures: A hard constraint makes the ask impossible

workflows.title: Log Constraints & Assumptions
workflows.summary: Pull every technical limit into one log, keep facts and guesses apart, confirm the hard ones with their owners and hand on the system context pack.

steps.title: Pull every limit into the log
steps.ask: From my brief summary, audit, data flow map and integration inventory, pull out every technical limit into constraint-log rows: C-## or A-## ID, the statement, area, hard or soft, and the source. Don't add anything that isn't in my documents.

lenses.note: Limits from the audit and integrations, not just the brief.
Hosting, region and platform limits.

steps.title: Tag assumptions & how to test them
steps.ask: Go through the log and challenge each constraint: does it have a source I could show someone? Re-tag anything that doesn't as an assumption, with a confidence (high / medium / low) and the cheapest way to test it.

uses.name: Facts are sourced, guesses are labelled
uses.ref: Facts are sourced, guesses are labelled

lenses.note: Each assumption has a cheap way to test it.

steps.title: Confirm hard constraints with owners
steps.ask: For each hard constraint, write a short confirmation request to its owner — the statement, its source, and a yes/no question — so I can get it confirmed in writing.

lenses.note: Security constraints confirmed by their owner.
Data-residency limits confirmed by the privacy officer.

steps.title: Assemble the system context pack
steps.ask: Assemble my system context pack: one paragraph per part (brief, audit, context diagram, data flows, integrations, constraints, open questions) with a link to the full document, and a short 'what this means for the next step' at the end.

lenses.note: Volume and latency limits carried into the pack.

steps.title: Pack accepted?
steps.ask: Review my system context pack as the tech lead would: could someone frame the problem from it without guessing? List what's missing or unsourced.

contract.rework: Unsourced entries → back to the log
exit: Pack accepted by the tech lead
contract.handoff: System context pack → 1.2 Frame the Technical Problem
traceability: C-## and A-## link to their source and to REQ-###

objectives: Give every assumption a confidence and a test
Confirm hard constraints with their owners
lessons.exercise: Write two constraints and two assumptions for the order-intake case, each with its source, and a test for each assumption. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: What makes something a constraint rather than an assumption?
options: It sounds important
It has a source you could show someone
The tech lead said so in passing
quiz.why: Constraints are sourced facts; everything else is an assumption until proven.

quiz.q: The client “prefers” Azure. Is that a hard constraint?
options: Yes
No — log it as a soft constraint unless an owner confirms it is required
Ignore it
quiz.why: Preferences are soft; only confirmed limits are hard.

lessons.prompt:
I'm working through "Log Technical Constraints & Assumptions" (Discover → Understand the Brief & the System) on my own project. Act as my assistant: draft and check, I decide.

Goal: Separate what you know about the system from what you're assuming, and hand on one consolidated technical picture.
Done looks like: A technical constraint & assumption log and the system context pack, accepted by the tech lead.

I'll attach or paste: Technical brief summary; System audit; Data flow map; Integration inventory; Technical question log.

Work through these steps with me, one at a time:
1. Pull every limit into the log → Technical constraint log
   From my brief summary, audit, data flow map and integration inventory, pull out every technical limit into constraint-log rows: C-## or A-## ID, the statement, area, hard or soft, and the source. Don't add anything that isn't in my documents.
2. Tag assumptions & how to test them → Technical constraint log
   Go through the log and challenge each constraint: does it have a source I could show someone? Re-tag anything that doesn't as an assumption, with a confidence (high / medium / low) and the cheapest way to test it.
3. Confirm hard constraints with owners → Technical constraint log
   For each hard constraint, write a short confirmation request to its owner — the statement, its source, and a yes/no question — so I can get it confirmed in writing.
4. Assemble the system context pack → System context pack
   Assemble my system context pack: one paragraph per part (brief, audit, context diagram, data flows, integrations, constraints, open questions) with a link to the full document, and a short 'what this means for the next step' at the end.
5. Pack accepted? (a decision — give me the options and a recommendation; I make the call)
   Review my system context pack as the tech lead would: could someone frame the problem from it without guessing? List what's missing or unsourced.

Produce: Technical constraint log; System context pack. Use clear headings I can paste into my document.

Before you finish, check it against: Constraints and assumptions kept apart; Every entry has a source; Every assumption has a test; Every entry sourced.

Ask me for anything you need instead of guessing. Keep it specific to my project.
